strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with multiple strong baselines (5 closed-source models, 15 open-source models, 6 existing methods)
Clear demonstration of scalability through Figure 3, showing consistent performance gains with increasing numbers of LLMs without saturation
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) and component analysis (Sections 4.5-4.6) quantifying contribution of each component
Elegant retrieval-based prior selection avoiding complex preprocessing, with practical black-box evaluation strategy enabling easy integration of new LLMs
Extensive reproducibility documentation including detailed hyperparameters, dataset splits, LLM specifications, and prompt designs in appendices
Strong empirical results with documented improvements over individual state-of-the-art models (GPT-4.1 +5.36%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet +12.73%)
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair computational comparison: SMACS requires ~16 LLM inference calls per query (7 referencers + aggregator with 8 aggregations) versus 1 call for closed-source baselines, yet frames results as model superiority rather than computational investment; no cost-normalized performance metrics provided

Limited novelty: combines straightforward techniques (RAG for model selection, standard perplexity/similarity metrics for response ranking, ensemble methods for diversity) without significant innovation; improvements over prior work are modest (Symbolic-MoE +5.14%, MoA +6.27%)

Hyperparameter selection lacks justification and rigor: multiple hyperparameters (K=7, N_sup_base=400, γ=0.95, λ=1.0) with no sensitivity analysis or principled tuning procedure disclosed; risk of overfitting if tuned on validation sets

No statistical rigor: single runs reported without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite stochastic LLM outputs (temperature=0.7); multiple runs needed to establish reliability

Incomplete efficiency analysis: paper acknowledges 'Lack of Efficiency Optimization' but provides no concrete latency, cost, or token-count measurements; practical deployment feasibility and cost-effectiveness unaddressed

Question bank design concerns: pre-processing cost unclear (evaluating 15 LLMs on all validation questions); generalization to out-of-distribution questions not analyzed; retrieval quality depends entirely on bank coverage

Posterior enhancement mechanism poorly justified: complex Equation (6) sampling distribution lacks clear motivation; K_drop=1 per iteration explores minimal response diversity; using perplexity as quality metric for arbitrary text generation is questionable (PPL designed for language modeling)
Limited failure analysis: no error analysis, case studies, or discussion of when/why method fails; which question types struggle; when running 7+ LLMs isn't worthwhile

Generalization concerns: experiments fixed to same 15-LLM set; no evaluation of performance with different LLM selections or diverse model architectures; reproducibility hampered by non-standard model names ('Claude-3.7-Sonnet', 'GPT-4.1') and unavailable unified question bank

Baseline and comparison issues: some baselines re-implemented (*Symbolic-MoE) possibly differing from originals; Self-Consistency baseline using only best validation LLM seems artificially weak; different experimental setups reduce fairness

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks covering multiple task categories (math, reasoning, instruction-following, code generation)
Demonstrates clear empirical performance improvements with detailed experimental results and ablation studies
Shows good scalability properties: performance improves consistently as more LLMs are added (Figure 3)
Provides analysis of prior selection via support question retrieval (Figure 4), showing reasonable domain-relevant results
Extensive implementation details and hyperparameter specifications aid reproducibility relative to some prior work
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair comparison: ensemble of 15 models compared against single closed-source models. Should compare ensemble-to-ensemble or account for computational cost explicitly. The title's claim of 'beating closed-source LLMs' is misleading.

Data leakage risk: validation sets from 8 benchmarks are pooled into question bank; RPS then retrieves from this bank at test time. Unclear if hyperparameters were tuned on same validation data, potentially inflating results.

Limited technical novelty: RPS is straightforward RAG application; EPE is basic combination of known techniques (response dropping, majority voting, perplexity-based selection) with only modest measured improvements (~0.5-1.5% per component).

Weak ablation validation: marginal improvements per component (Table 2); pairwise ranking metric (Table 3) shows only tiny gains over Symbolic-MoE; posterior enhancement improvements (Fig 5) are small; no justification for design choices (Eq. 6-7).

Methodological concerns: fixed Llama-3.3-70B aggregator adds non-transparent computational cost; hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning protocol unclear; small test sets (AIME ~30 questions) reduce reliability; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals.

Unaddressed computational cost: paper acknowledges 'lack of efficiency optimization' but fails to account for 15× inference cost in comparisons. No latency or token consumption analysis despite heavy computational footprint.
Question bank design raises reproducibility concerns: N_sup_base=400 selection strategy not clearly specified; no justification for tolerance threshold γ=0.95; no sensitivity analysis.
Missing fair comparisons: no comparison with (a) ensemble of closed-source models, (b) uniform ensemble of same 15 open-source models, (c) best-of-N sampling with equivalent compute.
Overclaimed contributions: abstract claims of 'pushing intelligence upper bound' and 'breaking through' are unsupported; ensemble superiority over single models is unsurprising and well-established.

Incomplete analysis: no error analysis, semantic diversity analysis, or failure case examination; no analysis of which model selections drive improvements; unclear how much gain comes from ensemble effects vs. RPS/EPE mechanisms specifically.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with consistent and substantial improvements (76.78% vs 65.66% closed-source average)
Impressive scaling behavior: convincingly demonstrates performance gains as more LLMs are added, addressing practical scalability concerns
Strong ablation studies (Table 2) clearly quantify individual component contributions with principled design
Good analysis of prior selection behavior (Fig. 4) showing meaningful cross-dataset retrieval patterns and correlation validation via pairwise ranking scores
Practical focus on continuous LLM integration without retraining, with extensive implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Retrieval-based selection is standard RAG application, EPE combines well-known techniques (dropping, multiple aggregations, scoring), and hybrid scoring is straightforward—primarily an engineering contribution

Critical experimental design issues: (1) Unfair comparison using strong aggregator (Llama-3.3-70B, which is best on most benchmarks) while baselines may not use same; (2) Potential data contamination from combining validation sets into question bank, creating information leakage and violating test-set integrity

Missing computational cost analysis despite computational overhead being prohibitive (K=7 references + n=8 aggregations): no latency, throughput, or cost-per-query comparison vs. single-model inference provided

Hyperparameter sensitivity completely unanalyzed: K=7, γ=0.95, n=8, λ=1.0 appear arbitrarily chosen with no justification or ablation studies across values; unclear if overfitted to these 8 benchmarks

Overstated claims: 'pushing upper bound of intelligence' is hyperbolic; claimed +2.04% gains over 'closed-source upper bound' are marginal, lack statistical significance testing and error bars, no analysis of variance across seeds

Generalization concerns: all benchmarks are structured academic tasks (math, code, QA); unclear performance on open-ended generation; aggregator selection sensitivity (Appendix A.4) suggests method is LLM-combination dependent

Incomplete baseline diversity and missing simpler alternatives: no comparison with weighted voting based on validation performance, no smaller efficient models, limited exploration of ensemble design space
Technical clarity issues: exponential weighting in Eq. 6 not justified, normalization of similarity and PPL scores in Eq. 7 unclear, embedding model choice (Linq-Embed-Mistral) unjustified

strengths: Impressive and comprehensive empirical results across 8 diverse benchmarks with substantial improvements over closed-source models (+11.12%) and open-source baselines (+17.12%)
Thorough experimental evaluation including ablation studies, component analysis, OOD performance, and statistical significance testing across multiple datasets
Clear demonstration of scalability with increasing number of LLMs (Figure 4) showing consistent performance gains without apparent saturation
Practical system with competitive cost ($8.11 vs $15.36) and reasonable latency (12.32s) despite computational complexity
Detailed analysis of system components including retrieval patterns (Fig. 5), prior-actual performance correlation (Table 4), and diversity-quality trade-offs (Fig. 6)
Comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Tables 11-13), and cost-effectiveness studies enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: RPS is straightforward RAG application to question bank, scoring mechanisms are standard, and EPE exploration is conventional prior-weighted sampling; contribution is primarily engineering/systems-level rather than algorithmic innovation
Critical dependence on question bank quality and diversity without principled construction guidelines; OOD performance degradation (Table 3) raises concerns about generalization to truly novel tasks

Experimental fairness concerns: different baseline configurations (Symbolic-MoE marked with *), task-specific prompts (Fig. 8) differing from baselines, fixed aggregator selected post-hoc, and artificial 'upper bound' baseline definitions

Hybrid scoring mechanism (Eq. 7) lacks strong justification: balance coefficient λ=1.0 set without sensitivity analysis, unconventional PPL formulation (1-PPL), and Appendix A.7's handling of numerical scale mismatch is hand-wavy

Reproducibility and scalability barriers: requires deployment of 15 LLMs with pre-computation of ~5,512 questions × 15 models, code not yet released, and prohibitive resource requirements for most researchers

Insufficient theoretical justification for core design choices: why should question-level retrieval similarity predict LLM capability match? Pairwise ranking score (Eq. 8) is convoluted without clear motivation
Missing analysis of failure cases, error categorization, and qualitative examples; no investigation of optimal team composition or which models complement each other best
Limited ablation on critical hyperparameters: tolerance coefficient γ=0.95, N_sup_base=400, K=7, n=8 choices lack justification; sensitivity analysis missing for different task types

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with thorough ablations and sensitivity analyses
Extensive reproducibility details including hyperparameters, implementation details, and prompts
Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements with good cost-efficiency analysis
Scalability analysis (Figure 4) showing performance gains with increasing numbers of LLMs
Reasonable out-of-domain experiments on multiple new datasets (Appendix A.6)
weaknesses: Fundamental methodological flaw: Question bank constructed from validation sets, enabling implicit information leakage from validation to test via retrieval mechanism
Unfair comparisons with closed-source models: SMCS uses 15+ forward passes while comparing against single LLM; claim of '+5.36% vs GPT-4.1' is misleading without accounting for computational budget
Limited technical novelty: RPS is standard RAG + scoring, EPE uses conventional aggregation and response scoring; combining existing techniques without fundamental innovations
Misuse of 'exploration-exploitation' terminology: Random dropping is not true exploration, and scoring is not RL exploitation; framing appears post-hoc
Question bank design undermines scalability claims: Adding new LLMs requires re-evaluating entire bank; requires pre-computation and creates data distribution coupling
Incomplete justification of design choices: Hybrid scoring (Eq. 7) with perplexity + similarity lacks motivation; no analysis of PPL correlation with correctness; λ=1.0 not justified
Circular hyperparameter tuning: All parameters appear tuned on validation data that contributed to question bank construction, raising generalization concerns
Insufficient comparison with routing baselines: Missing detailed comparisons with RouterDC, ZOOTER, and other prior-based methods; only Symbolic-MoE comparison in depth
Limited analysis of when/why approach works: No investigation of question difficulty, LLM combination effectiveness, or conceptual advantages over alternatives
Overclaimed contributions: Terms like 'significantly advancing performance frontier' and '+2.86% over upper bound' (averaging best-per-dataset) are vague or misleading

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear identification of scalability limitations in existing multi-LLM systems
Clever retrieval-based prior selection design that avoids complex preprocessing while enabling adaptive, instance-level LLM selection
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with strong consistent improvements over both closed-source (GPT-4.1, GPT-o3-mini) and open-source baselines
Excellent experimental rigor: thorough ablations, OOD generalization tests, statistical analysis, aggregator selection studies, cost-efficiency curves, and component contribution analysis
Clear scalability demonstration showing monotonic performance improvement with increasing number of LLMs (Fig. 4)
Practical feasibility with competitive cost ($8.11) and latency compared to proprietary models
Well-executed system design combining retrieval-based selection with exploration-exploitation-driven enhancement
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations and generally well-organized writing
weaknesses: Evaluation setup concern: unified question bank constructed from benchmark validation sets, creating potential distribution alignment bias toward test performance; baseline comparisons with prior work (Symbolic-MoE, MoA) may not use identical 15-LLM pools

Limited algorithmic novelty: RPS is essentially standard RAG applied to LLM selection; EPE combines existing techniques (perplexity, similarity, dropping); contribution is primarily system design rather than novel algorithms
Hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: K=7, n=8, λ=1.0, γ=0.95, etc. appear empirically tuned; fixed aggregator (Llama-3.3-70B) is task-dependent yet treated as universal

Perplexity scoring methodology: combining S_sim ∈ [0,1] with S_PPL ∈ [-∞,0] with λ=1.0 treats mismatched scales; assumption that perplexity (predictability) correlates with answer correctness is insufficiently justified; no learning of λ
Suspicious uniformity of improvements across all 8 benchmarks with no failure mode analysis, suggesting possible evaluation bias or overfitting to benchmark distributions
Reproducibility gaps: code not released (only promised); multiple LLM versions and embeddings complicate reproduction; unclear if task-specific prompts were tuned independently
Loose 'exploration-exploitation' framing: not formulated as formal multi-armed bandit problem; exploration phase is simply random dropping based on prior scores
Limited scalability demonstration: only shown up to 15 models; question bank may become bottleneck with many more LLMs; unclear if improvements persist to 50+models
Incomplete baselines: no comparison with recent routing methods despite citing RouterDC and GraphRouter; missing simple baselines like random or equal weighting

Generalization concerns: all evaluation on standardized benchmarks with objective answers; no evaluation on open-ended generation, real-world queries, or user studies; applicability to subjective correctness is unclear
